Matrix 2 has entries 37, 38, 39 in the first row, 40, 41, 42 in the second row, 43, 44, 45 in the third row. Matrix 3 has entries 46, 47, 48 in the first row, 49, 50, 51 in the second row, 52, 53, 54 in the third row. Row 3: Matrix 1 has entries 55, 56, 57 in the first row, 58, 59, 60 in the second row, 61, 62, 63 in the third row. Matrix 2 has entries 64, 65, 66 in the first row, 67, 68, 69 in the second row, 70, 71, 72 in the third row. Matrix 3 has entries 73, 74, 75 in the first row, 76, 77, 78 in the second row, 79, 80, 81 in the third row. End matrix.](images/a02_dequ15.png)

For example, the number 8 can be denoted as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1132</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![t sub 1132 equals 8](images/a02_dequ17.png)

This is because in the tensor <math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi></math>![T](images/MathcabEQ_0002.png), the element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1132</mn></msub></math>![t subscript 1132](images/a02_dequ18.png)is located in the first row (of matrices), first column (of matrices), third row (of scalars), and second column (of scalars).

[Figure A.2](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-2) illustrates how to locate the number 8 by “slicing” the tensor:

![FIGURE A.2 Visualization of a 4D tensor.](images/cappf002.png)

[FIGURE A.2](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-2) Visualization of a 4D tensor.

### Rank

The *rank* of a tensor, often called its *order*, is the number of indices or axes required to specify a particular element of the tensor (or the number of dimensions of the tensor as a multidimensional array):

*   **Rank 0**: A scalar (a single number) has rank 0.
*   **Rank 1**: A vector (a list of numbers) has rank 1.
*   **Rank 2**: A matrix (a 2D array of numbers) has rank 2.
*   **Higher ranks**: A tensor with rank 3 would require three indices to specify a component (e.g., a 3D array), rank 4 would need four, and so on.

In the previous example, the rank of the tensor T is 4 because you need four indices to locate a particular element.

## Statistics

Statistics help summarize and analyze data, providing insights into patterns, variability, and relationships. Fundamental concepts such as mean, median, standard deviation, and correlation are widely used in data preprocessing, evaluation, and feature engineering.

### Population and Samples

In statistics, a *population* indicates a complete dataset, whereas a *sample* is a subset of a dataset.

### Mean, Median, Mode

The arithmetic *mean* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi></math>![mu](images/a02_dequ19.png)is the average value of a dataset, calculated by summing all the values and dividing by the total number of elements. It provides a measure of central tendency but is sensitive to outliers.

The arithmetic mean <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi></math>![Greek letter mu](images/a02_dequ20.png)of a population comprised of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/a02_dequ21.png)data points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![x 1 , … , x n](images/a02_dequ22.png)can be calculated with the following formula:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle></math>![mu equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of x sub i, all divided by n](images/a02_dequ23.png)

The *median* represents the middle value of a sorted dataset and is more robust to extreme values than the mean. The *mode* is the most frequently occurring value in a dataset and is especially useful for categorical data.

### Standard Deviation

*Standard deviation* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></math>![sigma](images/a02_dequ24.png)measures how spread out the data is around the mean. A higher standard deviation indicates greater variability, whereas a lower one signifies that data points are closer to the mean. It is a vital metric in assessing the reliability and consistency of datasets.

The standard deviation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></math>![Sigma](images/a02_dequ25.png)of a population can be calculated with the following formula:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></math>![Sigma equals the square root of one over n times the sum from i equals 1 to n of left parenthesis x sub i minus mu right parenthesis squared.](images/a02_dequ26.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/a02_dequ27.png)is a variable that enumerates the data points, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![x sub i](images/a02_dequ28.png)denotes a data point, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi></math>![mu](images/a02_dequ29.png)is the arithmetic mean of the population, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/a02_dequ30.png)is the total number of data points in the population.

The standard deviation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/a02_dequ31.png)of a sample can be calculated with the following formula:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></msqrt></math>![s equals the square root of, fraction 1 over n minus 1, sum from i equals 1 to n of, open paren, x subscript i, minus, x bar, close paren, squared.](images/a02_dequ32.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/a02_dequ33.png)is a variable that enumerates the data points, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![x subscript i](images/a02_dequ34.png)denotes a data point, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![x bar](images/a02_dequ35.png)is the arithmetic mean of the sample, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/a02_dequ36.png)is the total number of data points in the sample.

### Covariance

*Covariance* is a measure of the relationship between two variables, indicating whether they tend to increase or decrease together. A positive covariance means the variables increase together, whereas a negative covariance means one decreases as the other increases. However, covariance does not indicate the strength of the relationship; correlation is used for that.

For a population, covariance is defined as follows:

<math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mrow><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle></math>![Cov left parenthesis cap x comma cap y right parenthesis equals n ary summation from i equals one to n over left parenthesis cap x sub i minus mu sub cap x right parenthesis times left parenthesis cap y sub i minus mu sub cap y right parenthesis divided by n](images/MathcabEQ_0003.png)

For a sample, covariance is defined as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover><mi>Y</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math>![This expression represents the covariance between two variables, X and Y. The covariance is calculated as follows: The sum from i equals 1 to n of the product of two terms. The first term is the difference between X subscript i and the mean of X. The second term is the difference between Y subscript i and the mean of Y. This sum is then divided by n minus 1. The formula is presented as a block and can be scrolled if it overflows.](images/a02_dequ38.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>![mu sub X](images/a02_dequ39.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math>![mu subscript Y](images/a02_dequ40.png)are the means of variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>X</mi></math>![X](images/a02_dequ41.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>Y</mi></math>![Y](images/a02_dequ42.png)for the population, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![X bar](images/a02_dequ43.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover><mi>Y</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![Y bar](images/a02_dequ44.png)are the sample means.

### Correlation

*Correlation* quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. The Pearson’s correlation coefficient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/a02_dequ45.png)between two variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>X</mi></math>![X](images/a02_dequ46.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>Y</mi></math>![Upper Y](images/a02_dequ47.png)ranges from −1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation), with 0 indicating no correlation. It is widely used in feature selection and understanding dependencies in data.

For a population, the correlation coefficient is defined as follows:

<math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math>![r equals Cov left parenthesis cap x comma cap y right parenthesis divided by normal sigma sub cap x times normal sigma sub cap y](images/MathcabEQ_0004.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>![Covariance of X and Y](images/a02_dequ49.png)is the population covariance, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>![sigma sub X](images/a02_dequ50.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math>![sigma subscript Y](images/a02_dequ51.png)are the standard deviations of the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>X</mi></math>![Capital X](images/a02_dequ52.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>Y</mi></math>![Uppercase Y](images/a02_dequ53.png), respectively.

For a sample, the correlation coefficient is defined as follows:

<math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math>![r equals Cov left parenthesis cap x comma cap y right parenthesis divided by s sub cap x times s sub cap y](images/MathcabEQ_0005.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>![Covariance of X and Y](images/a02_dequ55.png)is the sample covariance, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>![Sub X](images/a02_dequ56.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math>![Subscript s Y](images/a02_dequ57.png)are the standard deviations of the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>X</mi></math>![X](images/a02_dequ58.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>Y</mi></math>![Y](images/a02_dequ59.png), respectively.

### Outliers

*Outliers* are data points that deviate significantly from the rest of the dataset. They can result from variability in the data, errors in data collection, or rare events. Detecting and handling outliers is critical to prevent them from skewing analyses or distorting model performance.

### Histograms

*Histograms* are graphical representations of data distributions. They divide data into intervals (or bins) and show the frequency of values within each bin. Histograms are an intuitive way to visualize the shape of data, detect skewness, and identify potential outliers.

[Figure A.3](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-3) illustrates a histogram of normally distributed data.

![FIGURE A.3 Histogram of normally distributed data.](images/cappf003.png)

[FIGURE A.3](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-3) Histogram of normally distributed data.

## Probability Theory

Probability theory is the branch of mathematics that deals with quantifying the likelihood of events in experiments or random phenomena. It provides a framework to reason about uncertainty in data and models. In ML, probability is crucial for understanding distributions, making predictions, and modeling randomness.

 

### Probability as a Measure Function

Probability can be formally defined as a *measure function* that assigns a value to subsets of a sample space, denoted as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![The expression is simply the uppercase letter S.](images/a02_dequ60.png). A probability function satisfies the following axioms (Kolmogorov’s axioms):

*   **Axiom 1 (non-negativity)**: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>A</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![P of A is greater than or equal to 0](images/a02_dequ61.png)for all events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi></math>![A](images/a02_dequ62.png)in the sample space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![S](images/a02_dequ63.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![A subset of S](images/a02_dequ64.png)to denote <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi></math>![Uppercase A](images/a02_dequ65.png)is a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![S](images/a02_dequ66.png)).
*   **Axiom 2 (normalization)**: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>S</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![P S equals 1](images/a02_dequ67.png)(the probability of the sample space is 1).
*   **Axiom 3 (additivity)**: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8746;</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>A</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>B</mi></mfenced></math>![P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B](images/a02_dequ68.png)for any mutually exclusive events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi></math>![Capital A](images/a02_dequ69.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>B</mi></math>![B](images/a02_dequ70.png).

Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![S](images/a02_dequ71.png)be the sample space, the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. A **probability function** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi></math>![P](images/a02_dequ72.png)maps subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![S](images/a02_dequ73.png)(called *events*) to real numbers, such that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mfenced close="\]" open="\["><mn>0,1</mn></mfenced></math>![P colon script F right arrow closed interval 0 comma 1](images/a02_dequ74.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![Script F](images/a02_dequ75.png)is the set of all events (subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi></math>![S](images/a02_dequ76.png)), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>A</mi></mfenced></math>![P of A](images/a02_dequ77.png)represents the probability of event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi></math>![A](images/a02_dequ78.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8838;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi></math>![A subset or equal to S](images/a02_dequ79.png).

### Probability Distribution

A *probability distribution* is a mathematical description of the likelihood of different outcomes in a random experiment. It maps each possible outcome of an experiment to its probability. There are two types of distributions:

*   **Discrete distributions** Probabilities are assigned to distinct, separate outcomes in the discrete sample space by a *probability mass function* (PMF). The PMF assigns a probability to each specific outcome, ensuring that the sum of the probabilities of all possible outcomes equals 1.
*   For example, the Bernoulli distribution (described shortly) or rolling a die (described in the next section) has a PMF where each outcome (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) is assigned a specific probability.
*   **Continuous distributions** Probabilities are assigned to intervals of outcomes by a *probability density function* (PDF). The PDF describes the likelihood of a random variable falling within a particular range of values rather than assigning probabilities to specific points (because the probability of any single point in a continuous distribution is 0).
*   For example, the normal distribution (described shortly) uses a PDF to determine the probability over an interval, such as the likelihood that a value lies between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/a02_dequ81.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/a02_dequ82.png).

### Example: A Six-faced Die

A good example of a probability distribution is a standard six-faced die. Each face has an equal probability, leading to a discrete uniform distribution:

 <math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>6</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap p of cap a equals absolute value of cap a divided by absolute value of cap s comma cap s equals left curly bracket one comma two comma three comma four comma five comma six right curly bracket](images/MathcabEQ_0006.png)

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>A</mi></mfenced></math>![Absolute value of A](images/a02_dequ84.png)is the number of favorable outcomes in event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi></math>![A](images/a02_dequ85.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>S</mi></mfenced></math>![|S|](images/a02_dequ86.png)is the total number of outcomes in the sample space (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>S</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![Absolute value of S equals 6](images/a02_dequ87.png)).

For example, the probability of rolling a 5 (event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext>5</mtext></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![A equals set 5.](images/a02_dequ88.png)) is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>A</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![P of A equals 1 over 6](images/a02_dequ89.png)

##### Multiple Outcomes

The probability of rolling an even number (event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext>2</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>4</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>6</mtext></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![B equals the set containing 2, 4, 6.](images/a02_dequ90.png)) is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>B</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>B</mi></mfenced><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>S</mi></mfenced></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![P of B equals the fraction with absolute value of B over absolute value of S, which equals the fraction with numerator 3 and denominator 6, which equals the fraction with numerator 1 and denominator 2.](images/a02_dequ91.png)

##### Compound Events

The probability of rolling a number greater than 3 (event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext>4</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>5</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>6</mtext></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![C equals the set containing 4, 5, and 6](images/a02_dequ93.png)) is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>C</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>C</mi></mfenced><mfenced close="&#124;" open="&#124;"><mi>S</mi></mfenced></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![P of C equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue C EndAbsoluteValue Over StartAbsoluteValue S EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction equals StartFraction 3 Over 6 EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 EndFraction](images/a02_dequ94.png)

##### Complement Rule

The complement of event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi></math>![C](images/a02_dequ95.png)(rolling a number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![less than or equal to 3](images/a02_dequ96.png)) is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>c</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>P</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>C</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![P of C sub c equals 1 minus P of C equals 1 minus one half equals one half.](images/a02_dequ97.png)

##### Union of Events

The probability of rolling either an even number or a number greater than 3 (event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext>2</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>4</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>5</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mtext>6</mtext></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![D equals the set containing 2, 4, 5, and 6.](images/a02_dequ98.png)) is as follows:

<math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>6</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>5</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap p of cap d equals part 2 cap p of left curly bracket two comma four comma six right curly bracket plus cap p of left curly bracket five right curly bracket equals part 3 three divided by six plus one divided by six equals part 4 four divided by six equals part 5 two divided by three](images/MathcabEQ_0007.png)

##### Independent Events

If two dice are rolled, the outcome of the first die does not affect the outcome of the second die. For example, the probability of rolling a 6 on the first die and an even number on the second die is the product of the probabilities of each independent event:

<math class="a" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtext>6&#160;on&#160;1st die and even on&#160;2nd die</mtext><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>6</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>6</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>&#8901;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></mstyle></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap p of six on one st die and even on two nd die equals part 2 cap p of left curly bracket six right curly bracket dot operator cap p of left curly bracket two comma four comma six right curly bracket equals part 3 one divided by six dot operator one divided by two equals part 4 one divided by 12](images/MathcabEQ_0008.png) 

##### Simulation in Python

The following Python code simulates rolling a six-faced die 10,000 times using random sampling from the possible outcomes \[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\]. It then calculates the relative frequency of each outcome and plots a bar chart to represent the probability distribution of the die rolls visually. The chart shows how the frequencies approximate a uniform distribution due to the large sample size, demonstrating the concept of probability in action:

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
# Simulate rolling a 6-faced die 10,000 times
rolls = np.random.choice([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], size=10000)
unique, counts = np.unique(rolls, return_counts=True)
 
# Plot the relative frequency of each outcome
plt.bar(unique, counts / sum(counts), color='skyblue', edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Probability Distribution of Rolling a 6-Faced Die")
plt.xlabel("Die Face")
plt.ylabel("Relative Frequency")
plt.grid(axis='y')
plt.show()
```

[Figure A.4](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-4) shows the probability distribution.

![FIGURE A.4 Uniform probability distribution.](images/cappf004.png)

[FIGURE A.4](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-4) Uniform probability distribution.

 

### Normal Distribution

The normal distribution is one of the most widely used distributions in ML due to its natural occurrence in many real-world datasets (e.g., height, weight, test scores). It is symmetric, centered around its mean (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></math>![mu](images/a02_dequ103.png)), with a predictable spread determined by its standard deviation (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></math>![sigma](images/a02_dequ104.png)).

The central limit theorem reinforces its importance by stating that the mean of a sufficiently large number of independent, identically distributed variables will follow a normal distribution, regardless of the original data distribution.

Many ML algorithms assume data to be normally distributed to simplify computations. The PDF is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">&#960;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt></mfrac></mstyle><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msup><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></msup></math>![Function f of x equals 1 over square root of 2 pi sigma squared, times e to the power of minus 1/2 times the quantity x minus mu squared over sigma squared.](images/a02_dequ105.png)

The following Python program generates a plot of the PDF ([Figure A.5](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-5)):

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm
 
# Normal Distribution
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 1000)
mu, sigma = 0, 1
plt.plot(x, norm.pdf(x, mu, sigma))
plt.title("Normal Distribution")
plt.xlabel("Value")
plt.ylabel("Density")
plt.grid()
plt.show()
```

![FIGURE A.5 Normal probability density function bold open paren mu equals 0 comma sigma equals 1 bold close paren).](images/cappf005.png)

[FIGURE A.5](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-5) Normal probability density function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">&#956;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mstyle></math>![bold open paren mu equals 0 comma sigma equals 1 bold close paren](images/a02_dequ106.png)).

 

### Bernoulli Distribution

The Bernoulli distribution models binary outcomes (0 or 1) and is commonly used in ML to represent success/failure problems. Examples include determining whether an email is spam or classifying images as cat versus noncat. The key parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi></math>![The expression is simply the variable p.](images/a02_dequ109.png)represents the probability of success (1), whereas <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>p</mi></math>![1 minus p](images/a02_dequ111.png)represents the probability of a failure (0). It is widely used in logistic regression and binary classification tasks. The PMF is as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>1</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![P of X equals x, equals p to the power of x, times, quantity 1 minus p, close quantity, to the power of 1 minus x, for x in the set containing 0 and 1.](images/a02_dequ113.png)

The following Python program generates a plot of the PMF ([Figure A.6](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-6)):

```
from scipy.stats import bernoulli
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
# Bernoulli Distribution
p = 0.6
data = bernoulli.rvs(p, size=1000)
plt.hist(data, bins=2, edgecolor='k')
plt.title("Bernoulli Distribution (p = 0.6)")
plt.xlabel("Outcome")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.xticks([0, 1], ['0', '1'])
plt.grid()
plt.show()
```

![FIGURE A.6 Bernoulli probability mass function (bold italic p equals 0.6).](images/cappf006.png)

[FIGURE A.6](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-6) Bernoulli probability mass function (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mstyle></math>![bold italic p equals 0.6](images/a02_dequ114.png)).

 

## Calculus

Calculus is fundamental to understanding and implementing ML algorithms. Key aspects like derivatives and gradients are used to optimize models by minimizing errors (i.e., loss functions) or maximizing performance metrics (e.g., accuracy). For example:

*   **Derivatives** help measure changes and adjust parameters efficiently.
*   **Gradients** form the basis of parameter optimization techniques, such as gradient descent.
*   **Maxima and minima** are used to identify optimal solutions in model training.

By leveraging calculus, ML algorithms can adapt and learn from data through iterative optimization processes.

### Derivatives and Slope

*Derivatives* quantify the rate of change of a function with respect to its input, representing the slope of the function’s graph at a given point. In ML, this concept is critical for understanding how changes in parameters affect the output.

In its simplest form, the derivative of a single variable function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi></math>![function f](images/a02_dequ115.png)can be expressed as follows:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8242;</mi></msup><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>lim</mi><mrow><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mo>&#8289;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>![The derivative of f of x equals the limit as delta x approaches 0 of the fraction with numerator f of the quantity x plus delta x minus f of x, and denominator delta x.](images/a02_dequ116.png)

This formula expresses how a derivative—denoted as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8242;</mi></msup><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced></math>![f prime of x](images/a02_dequ117.png)—measures the rate at which a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![function f of x](images/a02_dequ118.png)changes as its input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi></math>![The expression is “x“.](images/a02_dequ119.png)changes. The term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![Delta x](images/a02_dequ120.png)represents a small change in the input, and the fraction calculates the ratio of the change in the function’s output (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced></math>![f of, open paren, x plus Delta x, close paren, minus f of, open paren, x, close paren](images/a02_dequ121.png)) to the change in input (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![Delta x](images/a02_dequ122.png)).

The limit as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#916;</mo><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![Delta x space right arrow 0](images/a02_dequ123.png)ensures that the derivative captures the instantaneous rate of change at a specific point on the curve of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced></math>![f of x](images/a02_dequ124.png). In simpler terms, it describes the slope of the tangent line to the function at any given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/a02_dequ125.png). This concept is crucial in ML for understanding how a small change in input (features) affects the outcome (prediction).

[Figure A.7](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-7) visually demonstrates the concept of derivative and slope with a simple function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![f of x equals x squared](images/a02_dequ126.png), showing its derivative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>![f prime of x equals 2x](images/a02_dequ127.png)at input point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x equals 0](images/a02_dequ128.png).

![FIGURE A.7 Derivative and slope (bold italic f of bold italic x equals bold italic x squared).](images/cappf007.png)

[FIGURE A.7](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-7) Derivative and slope (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></math>![bold italic f of bold italic x equals bold italic x squared](images/a02_dequ129.png)).

 

### Maxima and Minima

In ML, maxima and minima are essential for optimization, determining where a function (e.g., loss or objective function) is at its peak.

For nonlinear functions, the highest peak or the maximum value refers to the *maxima*, and the lowest peak or the lowest value refers to the *minima*. Put differently, the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/a02_dequ130.png)at which the derivative of a function is 0 is defined as the maxima or the minima.

Maxima and minima are the points where the value of the function remains constant: i.e., the change rate is 0.

The concepts of maxima and minima can be global or local, to indicate whether the peak applies to the entire domain of the function (global) or only to a specific neighborhood around a point (local).

More formally, a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x](images/a02_dequ133.png)has a local minima at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![x equals a](images/a02_dequ134.png)if there exists an interval <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![open paren, a minus h, comma, space, a plus h, close paren](images/a02_dequ135.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#62;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn></math>![h greater than 0](images/a02_dequ136.png), such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of a is less than or equal to f of x](images/a02_dequ137.png)for all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/a02_dequ138.png)in that interval.

[Figure A.8](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-8) visually illustrates these concepts, assuming the function is limited to a domain of positive real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x is greater than 0](images/a02_dequ139.png).

![FIGURE A.8 Maxima and minima visualizations, for Bold italic x greater than 0. (Bold italic f of bold italic x equals bold italic e to the power of minus bold italic x, multiplied by sine of 3 bold italic x).](images/cappf008.png)

[FIGURE A.8](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-8) Maxima and minima visualizations, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mstyle></math>![Bold italic x greater than 0.](images/a02_dequ140.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mfenced></msup><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8202;</mtext><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">\*</mi><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8202;</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">sin</mtext><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mfenced></mstyle></math>![Bold italic f of bold italic x equals bold italic e to the power of minus bold italic x, multiplied by sine of 3 bold italic x](images/a02_dequ141.png)).

 

### Partial Derivatives

In multivariable calculus, a *partial derivative* measures the rate of change of a function with respect to one variable, while keeping all other variables constant. This is essential in ML for optimizing functions involving multiple parameters, like loss functions.

More formally, for a multivariable function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>![f of, open paren, x sub 1, through, x sub n, close paren](images/a02_dequ142.png),

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>lim</mi><mrow><mo>&#916;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mo>&#8289;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#916;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#916;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></math>![Partial derivative of f with respect to x subscript i equals the limit as delta x subscript i approaches 0, of the quantity f of, open paren, x subscript 1, x subscript 2, ..., x subscript i plus delta x subscript i, ..., x subscript n, close paren, minus f of, open paren, x subscript 1, x subscript 2, ..., x subscript i, ..., x subscript n, close paren, divided by delta x subscript i.](images/a02_dequ143.png)

For example, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math>![function f of open paren x sub 1, x sub 2 close paren equals x sub 1 squared plus x sub 2 squared](images/a02_dequ144.png),

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![Partial derivative of f with respect to x subscript 1 equals 2 x subscript 1, partial derivative of f with respect to x subscript 2 equals 2 x subscript 2.](images/a02_dequ145.png)

Partial derivatives form the components of the gradient, which is key in optimization.

 

### Gradient

The *gradient* of a function is a vector containing all its partial derivatives. It points in the direction of the steepest ascent of the function.

More formally, for a multivariable function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>![f of, open paren, x sub 1, comma, horizontal ellipsis, comma, x sub n, close paren](images/a02_dequ146.png),

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="\]" open="\["><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced></math>![The gradient of f of x sub 1, x sub 2, through x sub n equals the vector of partial derivatives start fraction partial f over partial x sub 1 end fraction through start fraction partial f over partial x sub n end fraction.](images/a02_dequ147.png)

For example, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math>![The function f of x 1, x 2 equals x 1 squared plus x 2 squared.](images/a02_dequ148.png),

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="\]" open="\["><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8706;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="\]" open="\["><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></msub><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>![Gradient of f at (x₁, x₂) equals \[start fraction, partial f over partial x₁, end fraction, start fraction, partial f over partial x₂, end fraction\] equals \[2x₁, 2x₂\].](images/a02_dequ149.png)

In ML, the gradient is used to calculate the direction to adjust model parameters during optimization.

### Gradient Descent

Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts parameters to minimize a function (e.g., loss function). It uses the gradient to determine the direction and magnitude of parameter updates.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>-</mo><mtext>&#951;</mtext><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></math>![x subscript new, equals x subscript old, minus, eta, nabla, f open parenthesis x subscript old close parenthesis](images/a02_dequ150.png)

where

*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi></math>![Greek letter eta](images/a02_dequ151.png)is the learning rate hyperparameter (step size).
*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced></math>![Nabla f of x](images/a02_dequ152.png)is the gradient of the function.

This process is repeated until convergence: i.e., when updates become negligible or the function reaches its minimum.

[Figure A.9](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-9) visually illustrates the gradient descent convergence process for the single-variable function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![f of x equals x squared](images/a02_dequ153.png).

![FIGURE A.9 Gradient descent convergence process (bold-italic f of bold-italic x equals bold-italic x squared).](images/cappf009.png)

[FIGURE A.9](#a02.xhtml#rc0-fig-9) Gradient descent convergence process (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced close=")" open="("><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></math>![bold-italic f of bold-italic x equals bold-italic x squared](images/a02_dequ154.png)).

In [Figure A.9](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-9):

*   Steps 0, 1, and 2 are explicitly annotated with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></math>![Subscript x old](images/a02_dequ155.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f prime of x](images/a02_dequ156.png).
*   All steps beyond 3 are visually marked on the function line but are not annotated to maintain readability.
*   Starting from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![x equals 8](images/a02_dequ157.png)with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mtext>&#951;</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math>![Eta equals 0.2](images/a02_dequ158.png), the algorithm takes 10 iterations to converge, based on the number of steps shown.
*   By the 10th step, the changes in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/a02_dequ159.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x](images/a02_dequ160.png)are small enough to indicate convergence near the global minimum (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x equals 0](images/a02_dequ161.png)).

For your reference, the following Python code shows the plot illustrated in [Figure A.9](#a02.xhtml#c0-fig-9):

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
# Define the function and its gradient
def func(x):
    return x**2  # f(x) = x²
 
def gradient(x):
    return 2 * x  # Gradient: f'(x) = 2x
 
# Gradient descent parameters
learning_rate = 0.2
x = 8  # Initial point
steps = [x]  # To store the points during the descent
 
# Perform gradient descent
for _ in range(10):
    x_new = x - learning_rate * gradient(x)  # Gradient Descent Update
    steps.append(x_new)  # Track each step
    x = x_new  # Update x for the next iteration
 
# Generate data for the function
x_vals = np.linspace(-10, 10, 100)
y_vals = func(x_vals)
 
# Plot the function and gradient descent steps
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
plt.plot(x_vals, y_vals, label='f(x) = x²', color='black', linewidth=1.5)  # Function plot
 
# Annotate only the first 3 steps
for i, step in enumerate(steps[:3]):  # Only the first 3 steps
    gradient_at_step = gradient(step)
    plt.scatter(step, func(step), color='grey', zorder=5)  # Plot step points
    plt.annotate(f"Step {i}\n"
                 f"x_old={step:.2f}\n"
                 f"f'(x)={gradient_at_step:.2f}",
                 (step, func(step)),  # Arrow start
                 xytext=(8, func(step)),  # Arrow end (fixed on the right)
                 arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', arrowstyle="->"),
                 fontsize=8)
 
# Mark steps > 3 but don't annotate them
for step in steps[3:]:
    plt.scatter(step, func(step), color='grey', zorder=5)  # Mark remaining steps
 
# Final point annotation
plt.scatter(steps[-1], func(steps[-1]), color='black', zorder=5, label='Final Point (Convergence)')
 
# Add learning rate annotation
plt.text(-8, 60, f"Learning Rate: η = {learning_rate}", fontsize=10, bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.7))
 
# Axis and labels
plt.axhline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.7)  # Horizontal axis
plt.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.7)  # Vertical axis
plt.legend()
plt.title("Gradient Descent Visualization with First 3 Steps Annotated")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("f(x)")
plt.grid(color='grey', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.5)
plt.show()
```
